'''''Circaea lutetiana''''', known as '''broad-leaved enchanter's nightshade''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a [[plant]] in the evening primrose family, [[Onagraceae]].

The genus name comes from the enchantress [[Circe]] of Greek mythology and the specific designation is derived from [[Lutetia]], the Latin name for Paris, which was sometimes referred to as the "Witch City". Despite its name it is not especially toxic, but contains a lot of the [[astringent]] [[tannin]].<ref>[http://www.alchemy-works.com/info_enchanters_nightshade.html Alchemy Works] Accessed April 2014</ref>

==Description==
[[File:CircaeaLutetiana2.jpg|thumb|''Circaea lutetiana'' showing flowers and burrs]]
''Circaea lutetiana'' is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous plant]] with opposite, simple [[leaf|leaves]], on slender, green stems. The flowers are white, borne in summer. It grows {{Convert abbreviated|20 to 60|cm}}, rarely up to {{Convert abbreviated|75|cm}} high.<ref>[http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o548-enchantersnightshade.php Natural England.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110810184652/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o548-enchantersnightshade.php |date=2011-08-10 }}  Accessed July 2011</ref>

The leaves are rounded or slightly notched at the base, they narrow gradually to the pointed tip and are not strongly toothed, but have [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sinuate sinuate] edges. The leaf stalks are equally hairy all round.<ref>[http://www.english-country-garden.com/flowers/enchanters-nightshade.htm English Country Garden] Accessed July 2011</ref>

The flower has 2 notched petals, 2 stamens and a 2-lobed stigma. The open flowers are well spaced along the stalk and there are no bracts at the base of individual flower stalks. The fruit consists of 2 equal cells, and usually sets seed. The flower stalks become angled downwards before fruiting.<ref>[http://www.plant-identification.co.uk/skye/onagraceae/circaea-lutetiana.htm Plant Identification  UK] Accessed July 2011</ref> The fruit is a small [[bur]] of 3.5–5 mm<ref name=rhoa>{{cite book |last1=Rhoads |first1=Ann |last2=Block |first2=Tim |title=The Plants of Pennsylvania|date=5 September 2007 |isbn=978-0-8122-4003-0|edition=2nd}}</ref> which aids the plant's dispersal via [[zoochory]].

In winter the aerial parts die off leaving an underground [[rhizome]].

''[[Circaea alpina]]'' will [[hybrid biology|hybridize]] with ''Circaea lutetiana'' producing sterile offspring that persists in vegetative colonies.<ref name="rhoa" />

==Distribution==
The plant is native to Europe, Middle Asia, and Siberia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=CILU|title=Plants Profile for Circaea lutetiana (broadleaf enchanter's nightshade)|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=2016-06-26}}</ref> North American populations are now considered to be a separate species, ''[[Circaea canadensis]]''. It grows in woods in deep shade and moist environments on nitrogen-containing clay.

==Gardening==
It is cultivated as an ornamental garden plant. It prefers a shaded position in rich, moist soil.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/61781/Circaea-lutetiana/Details | title = ''Circaea lutetiana'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 28 June 2021}}</ref> The [[cultivar]] 'Caveat Emptor' has leaves that are heavily mottled pink.
